strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper provides both a corpus-level token-entropy analysis (6.8% vs 18.5% high-entropy token retention) and a controlled toy experiment isolating why reverse-KL policy-gradient rewards become unstable when the teacher distribution is high-entropy, giving good intuition before presenting the method.

The proposed fix (Eq. 9) is simple, easy to implement, and directly targeted at the diagnosed failure mode: reverse KL is retained where it is efficient (low teacher entropy) and forward KL is added only where diversity preservation matters (high teacher entropy), with a practical top-k approximation (Appendix F) to control the extra compute/memory cost of forward KL.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation: three model scales (0.6B/1.7B/4B), six math benchmarks, out-of-domain evaluation (GPQA, MMLU-Pro, AlpacaEval), Pass@k curves up to k=128, entropy-threshold and forward-KL-placement ablations, comparisons to entropy-bonus/advantage-shaping baselines, and an additional Llama-family experiment showing the approach is not architecture-specific.

The mechanistic explanation for the gains is corroborated by multiple complementary diagnostics (entropy histograms, forward-KL-at-high-entropy curves, top-k/top-1 change-rate metrics), which strengthens the causal story rather than just reporting benchmark deltas.
weaknesses: Reported gains are often small and inconsistent: several cells in Table 2 show EOPD tied with or slightly worse than OPD (e.g., Minerva Avg@8 for the 4B model: 40.08 vs 39.71; AIME24 Avg@8 for the 4B model: 18.33 vs 17.92; AMC23 Pass@8 for the 0.6B model: 57.50 vs 55.00), and the headline average improvements are computed over very small, high-variance benchmarks (AIME24/25 have only 30 questions each), yet no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported for the main results table, making it hard to assess whether the improvements are robust or within noise.

The method requires querying the teacher for distributional information (entropy and top-k logits) at every generated token during rollout, which adds non-trivial extra teacher queries and memory relative to standard on-policy distillation that only needs a single log-probability per token; the paper does not report wall-clock/compute overhead comparisons to substantiate the claim that on-policy training efficiency is preserved.

The entropy threshold tau is only tuned/ablated on the 1.7B model on two benchmarks (Table 5); it is unclear how sensitive the method is across model scales, datasets, or teacher/student capacity gaps, and no guidance is given for selecting tau in new settings without a validation sweep.

The core idea of blending forward and reverse KL based on a distributional statistic is conceptually close to prior interpolation/adaptive-divergence approaches (e.g., GKD's mixed-KL training, f-divergence distillation, TAID), and the paper's main technical novelty is the entropy-thresholded gating rule; the full forward KL and random forward KL ablations in Table 6 show EOPD's advantage over naive mixing is real but modest, somewhat limiting the perceived originality.

Baseline comparisons mix paradigms with different information/supervision (GRPO uses only scalar verifiable rewards without any teacher distribution, while EOPD/OPD/KD use dense teacher signals), and GRPO sometimes outperforms EOPD (e.g., several Avg@8 entries for 0.6B/4B), which is not deeply discussed and could mislead readers about the relative merits of teacher-distillation vs. RL-from-scratch approaches under matched compute.

strengths: Clear motivation and diagnosis of a real problem: the paper convincingly shows (via both a controlled toy experiment and token-entropy histograms on real models) that reverse-KL-based on-policy distillation causes diversity collapse and unstable gradients at high-entropy teacher tokens.

The proposed method (entropy-gated mixture of reverse and forward KL) is simple, well-motivated by the diagnosis, and computationally cheap: overhead is reported as only ~4.5% extra training time and modest memory (7.37x more efficient than full forward KL), with no extra teacher queries needed.

Extensive empirical validation: three model scales (0.6B/1.7B/4B), six math benchmarks, out-of-domain evaluation (GPQA, MMLU-Pro, AlpacaEval), Pass@k curves up to k=128, and a battery of ablations (τ, α, top-k, forward-KL placement) plus comparisons to many relevant baselines (GKD, entropy bonus, advantage shaping, BD-KD, AKL, ToDi).
Additional experiments on a different model family (Llama-3.2-3B/3.1-8B) support generalizability of the approach beyond Qwen3.
Good implementation transparency in the appendix (hyperparameters, chat templates, compute setup), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Absolute performance gains are often modest and inconsistent across benchmarks/metrics — e.g., Minerva Avg@8 for the 4B model actually decreases with EOPD (40.08→39.71), and several AIME25 Avg@8/Pass@8 differences are within likely noise, which weakens the claim of 'consistent' improvement.

No variance/error bars or multiple seeds are reported for the main Table 2 results (unlike the toy experiment, which uses 3 seeds), despite math benchmarks like AIME24/25 having very few problems (30) and high evaluation variance; this makes it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported gains.

The core idea—blending mode-seeking and mode-covering divergences based on a teacher discrepancy/uncertainty signal—overlaps conceptually with prior adaptive-KL methods (BD-KD, AKL, ToDi, F-divergence blends) cited in related work; while the paper compares against these, the novelty is comparatively incremental (a threshold-based gate on entropy versus other discrepancy measures).

The forward KL term is only approximated via a re-normalized top-k teacher distribution rather than the true forward KL, and while a probability-mass/memory tradeoff is shown, there is no direct ablation quantifying how much this approximation affects final performance versus an (expensive) full-vocabulary forward KL baseline (only a 'Full' forward-KL-at-all-positions baseline is given, not full-vocab vs top-k at the same positions).

The causal link between preserved high-entropy-token diversity and downstream accuracy gains is presented largely through correlational evidence (entropy histograms, forward-KL-at-high-entropy curves) rather than a more direct causal analysis (e.g., ablating diversity while controlling for other factors).

Hyperparameters τ and α, while shown to be reasonably robust in ablations, still require selection, and the analysis is limited to a single model (1.7B) and few benchmarks (MATH500, AMC23, AIME24/25), leaving open how sensitivity generalizes to other scales/domains.
